cues.text: Section six: SLAs, OLAs and service performance.
A service level agreement, or SLA, establishes agreed service commitments, responsibilities, measurement rules and review arrangements.
An operational level agreement, or OLA, coordinates the internal teams that support those commitments.
An underpinning contract establishes the obligations of suppliers.
Consider an example.
A customer SLA requires critical incidents to be restored within four hours.
The network team's OLA requires investigation within 30 minutes, and a cloud supplier's contract requires escalation support within one hour.
The point is that internal and external commitments must all support the customer target.
Next, three related terms.
A service level indicator, or SLI, measures actual performance.
A service level objective, or SLO, sets a target.
An SLA formalises agreed commitments.
For instance, the successful request percentage is an SLI.
A figure of 99.9 percent successful requests is an SLO.
The customer agreement may then specify consequences when that target is missed.
Now the availability formula.
Availability equals the agreed service time minus downtime, divided by the agreed service time, multiplied by 100 percent.
Here is a worked example.
For a 30-day service period running 24 hours a day, there are 720 hours.
If downtime is 3.6 hours, availability is 99.5 percent.
At 99.9 percent availability, the downtime allowance over the same period is 43.2 minutes.
Always check whether planned maintenance is excluded by the agreement.
Moving to reliability.
Reliability concerns consistent, failure-free operation.
Mean time between failures, or MTBF, estimates the average operating time between failures for repairable systems.
Mean time to repair or restore, or MTTR, measures the average recovery duration, and its precise definition depends on the organisation.
For example, suppose a repairable service has an MTBF of 99 hours and an MTTR of one hour.
Approximate steady-state availability equals MTBF divided by the sum of MTBF and MTTR.
That is 99 divided by 100, which gives 99 percent.
This assumes compatible definitions and stable conditions.
Finally, other key performance indicators include response time, throughput, error rate, first contact resolution, or FCR, customer satisfaction, or CSAT, backlog, and SLA attainment.
If 92 of 100 eligible tickets meet their targets, attainment is 92 percent.
And note that a rise in page-load latency is directly reflected in response time, not in MTBF or FCR.
